input.description: Count how many settings OrcaSlicer defines per scope and list the settings whose edits trigger special handling in the settings tab

content.text:
The project does record a justification for the small list, but it is about keeping the app from misbehaving, not about any setting being physically dangerous. I found no place that sorts settings into "safe" and "dangerous" for the print or the printer, so that second half below is my own reading of the code, labelled as such.

## What the record says

The list currently allows 41 of the 356 process settings OrcaSlicer defines (plus 34 of 128 filament settings and 35 of 113 printer settings).

**The original decision (commit 77c0c6a3c4, 2026-09-04).** The handoff document for the settings tools listed this as a decision "already made", not open for debate: reading covers every setting, but changing "starts with a reviewed allowlist" of seven keys. It added: "Expand the list only after the real-adapter tests cover the option type, dependency behavior, and visible UI update for each new key."

**The stated reason is one specific hazard.** The same document, and now the tool guide (`agent-docs/jusprin/mcp-tool-extension-guide.md`, section "The process normalizer can open dialogs and rewrite values"), explains it. After any settings change, OrcaSlicer re-checks the whole configuration. Some of its rules:

- **open a pop-up** and wait for an answer. A pop-up during a tool call freezes the app while the request waits.
- **silently change another setting.** Then the tool's report of what it did is wrong unless that rewrite was predicted.

So each key is admitted only after someone has read OrcaSlicer's rule code for every place that key is used and added a test proving no pop-up appears. The guide says a rule found later that a tool can trigger "is a defect in the preview. It is not behavior to accept."

**The second reason, for printer and filament settings (commit 0412386910, 2026-09-29).** Those lists deliberately leave out settings that decide which printer, nozzle, or extruder count is in use (bed shape, nozzle size, extruder count, printer model). The guide's reason: those decide which filament and process profiles are compatible, and changing them belongs to the printer setup tools, not a settings edit.

**What is not recorded anywhere:** why these 41 and not others. The list grew from 7 to 40 in one commit (c35dcfcd20) that added "supports, adhesion, seam and speeds", with no note on what was considered and skipped. The product definition talks about the person keeping control of "consequential real-world effects", but it ties that to sending a print, not to individual settings.

In short: the list is small because each key costs an audit and a test, and only the keys someone needed for a tested task were paid for. It is a "prove it is safe before allowing it" list, not a "these are the only safe ones" list.

## My guess at what is actually dangerous

This is inference from reading the code, not a recorded decision.

**1. Settings that make the app misbehave (the documented hazard).** These have pop-up rules in OrcaSlicer's checker:
- layer height (zero, or above the printer's maximum)
- ironing spacing, first layer height
- XY hole and contour compensation, elephant foot compensation
- spiral vase
- alternate extra wall with vertical shell thickness
- scarf seam start height
- infill lock depth
- fuzzy skin mode with the classic wall generator

The existing guard already refuses the bad combinations for all of these, which is why spiral vase was cheap to add. Most of the others are probably equally cheap.

**2. Settings that can harm the printer or the print.** Nothing in the code treats these specially, but they are where I would want a human look:
- **Custom G-code** (start, end, layer change, filament change). This is raw machine commands. It is already on the printer and filament lists, which surprised me given how cautious the process list is.
- **Temperatures.** Already allowed on the filament list. Too hot can damage a hotend or release fumes; too cold jams.
- **Machine limits** (maximum speeds, accelerations, jerk). Already allowed on the printer list. Wrong values cause skipped steps or crashes into the frame.
- **Retraction and Z offset.** Already allowed. A wrong Z offset can drive the nozzle into the bed.
- **Print sequence "by object"**, which needs clearance around the print head or it collides with finished parts.
- **Volumetric speed and flow**, which cause under-extrusion or jams.

**3. Settings that are harmless but were never needed.** Line widths, accelerations within the process, ironing, bridge settings, small-perimeter speeds, and most of the remaining 300 or so. These can produce a bad print, but nothing worse, and the slice report would show it.

## What I take from this

The caution is uneven. The process list is the tightest, yet process settings are mostly in group 3. The printer and filament lists are looser, yet they hold most of group 2. That fits the record: the gate was designed around pop-ups, and physical risk was never the criterion.

If you want the assistant to be more capable, the cheapest gain is admitting more group 3 process settings in batches, since the audit for each is short. If you want it to be safer, the place to look is group 2, which is already open.

| c35dcfcd20 (2026-09-16) | Grew the list to 40 settings | **Claude** (Opus 5), running on the Windows test VM | Not available on this Mac | See below |
| 0412386910 (2026-09-29) | Added the printer and filament lists | **Claude Code** (Opus 5.5) | "Tool refusal in printer mode switching" | Entire's checkpoint record names the agent and session; that session's transcript contains the commit command |

## The middle commit

The agent is certain, the session title is not recoverable from here. The commit carries a "Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5" line and has no Entire checkpoint. No Claude or Codex session on this Mac ran that commit. What I did find:

- A Claude session here titled **"MCP tools design docs"** (Sept 15 to 17) wrote a handoff file and copied it to the `jusprin-win-test` Windows VM.
- A later session here titled **"Journey tools review and testing"** opens with "a dev finished the work spec'd in" that handoff.
- The commit's timestamp is in UTC, unlike your Mac's commits.

So my reading is that a Claude Code session on the Windows VM made the commit. That session's record lives on the VM, if it still exists.

## What Entire could and could not do

- **Search does not work for this repository.** `entire search` fails with "no matching repositories found for TheSpaghettiDetective/JusPrin (is the repo mirrored to Entire?)".
- **The first commit predates Entire.** Entire was added to the repository on 2026-09-05, one day after it.
- **The installed command could not open the one checkpoint that exists.** `entire checkpoint explain` said "no checkpoint or commit found" for 0412386910, even though the commit names checkpoint `01M3PV7YBJA43V1QQ2YCTY7Q1G`. I read that checkpoint's record directly from where Entire stores it on GitHub. Your Entire is version 0.10.5 and it reports 0.11.4 is available; I do not know whether upgrading fixes this.
- **Entire does not store session titles.** It stores the agent, model, session id and prompts. The titles above come from the Claude and Codex apps' own records, matched by session id.

<pasted_content id="757f">
The agent could search and read every applicable setting. Writing was initially limited because changing an Orca setting can:

* Open a modal dialog and block the GUI thread.
* Silently rewrite dependent settings.
* Affect slicing, dirty state, saving, and revert behavior.
* Have different Undo semantics.
* Conflict with simultaneous GUI edits.

Each writable key therefore had to be traced through Orca’s normalizers and handlers, then tested for native UI updates, dependencies, atomic application, stale-state protection, and undo/revert behavior. See [mcp-tool-extension-guide.md (line 679)](/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/agent-docs/jusprin/mcp-tool-extension-guide.md:679).
The policy was: start with a small proven write surface, then expand key by key after real-adapter tests. This prevented the tool from hanging on dialogs or claiming one result while Orca silently produced another. The hazard audit explains those risks in [mcp-tool-extension-guide.md (line 880)](/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/agent-docs/jusprin/mcp-tool-extension-guide.md:880).

content.text:
Of the five original reasons, four are now handled by general machinery that works for any setting, so they no longer justify admitting settings one at a time. Only the first (pop-up dialogs) still depends on which setting is changed, and for process settings even that is already guarded across the whole configuration. This comes from reading the current code on `jusprin-newui`; I did not run a sweep that changes every setting.

## The five reasons today

| Original reason | Still a reason to vet each setting? | What handles it now |
|---|---|---|
| Opens a pop-up and blocks the app | **Partly** (details below) | A guard refuses, before applying, any configuration that would trigger a pop-up |
| Silently rewrites other settings | **No** | Preview runs OrcaSlicer's own rule code on a copy and reports any rewrite. Apply then compares every setting before and after and reports anything the preview missed |
| Affects slicing, unsaved state, saving, revert | **No** | Every change goes through OrcaSlicer's own settings tab (`Tab::load_config`), which does all of that the same way for any setting |
| Different Undo behaviour | **No** | Undo depends on where the setting lives (preset or object), not on which setting it is. The result states it either way |
| Conflicts with simultaneous edits in the app | **No** | Every apply is tied to the project revision and to the exact "before" values it previewed, and fails cleanly if either moved |

## Pop-ups: what is still true

**Process settings: already covered for all of them.** OrcaSlicer's process rule code has 13 live places that open a pop-up. The guard (`check_process_dialogs`) has a matching refusal for each one, and it checks the whole configuration after the change, not only the settings on the allow-list. So changing a process setting that is not on the list could not open one of these pop-ups either. The spiral vase fix worked for exactly this reason.

**Filament and printer settings: less certain.** Their guards were written only for the settings on their lists. I confirmed the filament tab has one pop-up path on this route and it is covered. I did not go through the printer tab exhaustively.

**A general safety net now exists but is not used here.** Since the allow-list was written, the fork gained a way to intercept any OrcaSlicer pop-up and answer it automatically (it is used when opening files). The settings apply step does not use it. If it did, a missed pop-up would no longer freeze the app.

## What still does depend on the setting

These are not in the original five, but they are the real per-setting concerns I found:

- **Warnings the app gives only when a person edits the field.** About ten process settings have their own pop-up in the settings tab's edit handler, which a tool change skips. Examples: turning off the prime tower with smooth timelapse on, choosing "by object" print order, precise Z height with a prime tower, support filament choices. A tool change would not freeze, but it would quietly skip a question the app considers worth asking.
- **Settings a plate can override.** Eight settings (print order, bed type, spiral vase and others) can be set per plate, in which case changing the process value has no effect on that plate.
- **Post-processing scripts.** The process setting `post_process` names a program that runs on the computer when G-code is exported. I confirmed it is currently refused. It should stay refused whatever else is opened up, because the tool endpoint has no login.

## Seen in passing

The read tool returned the printer's "API Key / Password" and "Password" fields. They were empty in the test profile, so I have not shown that a real stored secret comes back. I left a follow-up task chip for that.

## What this means

The key-by-key audit made sense when it was the only protection. Today it mostly re-proves things the general machinery already guarantees. A more fitting rule for process settings would be the reverse: allow everything, except a short named list (the ten or so with skipped warnings, the plate-overridable ones, and `post_process`). That is a policy change for you to decide, and I would want the every-setting sweep run before making it.

content.text:
I read the code for each point. All of this is from reading the current source on `jusprin-newui`; I did not run new tests for it.

## 1. Filament and printer pop-ups: now certain

I read every function the tools pass through on those two tabs: loading a batch, refreshing, switching to another filament, and saving.

**Filament tab: three pop-ups exist on this route, all three are guarded.**
- Max volumetric speed below 0.5 (checked on every update).
- First-layer temperature too far from the other layers' (asked on save; 30 °C for the nozzle, 15 °C for a plate). The guard uses the same numbers.
- "You have unsaved changes" when switching to another filament while the open one has unsaved edits.

**Printer tab: one pop-up exists, and it is guarded.** Firmware retraction combined with a wipe that retracts less than 100% first.

**One silent rewrite on the printer tab.** "Manual filament change" is switched off when the printer is not single-extruder multi-material. Preview does not predict it, but the after-apply comparison reports it.

As with process settings, these guards inspect the whole resulting configuration, not just the allow-listed settings. The many other filament pop-ups (chamber temperature, nozzle temperature range, bed temperature difference) sit in the edit-field handlers, which a tool change never runs.

## 2. Risks of using the automatic pop-up answering for settings

It is already used for the file-open and delete tools, so there is precedent. Four risks, in order of importance:

- **It trades a freeze for a quiet change of plan.** The automatic answer is "No", or "OK" when that is the only button. In these dialogs that still makes OrcaSlicer rewrite something. For example, "No" on the fuzzy-skin question switches the fuzzy-skin mode, and the OK-only ones reset the value you just set. The tool would have applied something different from what was previewed. So when it fires, the apply should fail and roll back, or at least say so loudly.
- **It can hide regressions.** Today's test counts pop-ups that appear on screen. An intercepted pop-up never appears, so that test would pass while a rule had been missed. Tests would need to assert that nothing was intercepted.
- **It does not catch everything.** It only sees pop-ups opened through OrcaSlicer's own dialog class during the call. It misses ones opened a moment later by a queued event, and native file pickers. I found none of those on the settings route.
- **A dialog that re-asks until it gets "Yes" would loop forever.** I saw none on this route.

My view: worth adding as a backstop behind the existing guards, never as a replacement for them.

## 3. The edit-time questions: who can answer them

Most are technical dependencies the assistant can handle, if the tool tells it about them. Two belong to the user.

| Question OrcaSlicer asks | Who can answer |
|---|---|
| Support interface material: "apply the recommended companion settings?" | Assistant. It should simply send them together, like spiral vase |
| Prime tower off while smooth timelapse or clumping detection needs it | Assistant. A pure dependency |
| Prime tower together with precise Z height "may cause slicing errors" | Assistant |
| Smooth timelapse without a prime tower: "enable the prime tower?" | Assistant, once it is known that a timelapse is wanted |
| Infill rotation on a pattern not designed for it | Assistant |
| Layer height outside the nozzle's limits | Assistant. Already refused by the guard |
| Non-soluble material for the support base "not recommended" | Mostly assistant, but it depends on which spools are really loaded |
| "By object" on a bed-slinger printer disables timelapse | User, mildly: do they want the timelapse? |
| "Make overhangs printable" changes the model's shape | **User.** Only they know whether exact dimensions or fit matter |
| Long retraction on filament cut: experimental, may raise clog risk | **User.** It is accepting a risk to their printer |

So the right treatment is the spiral vase pattern: the preview reports the condition and names the companion settings, and the assistant decides or asks. None needs to be a hard refusal except the two user ones, where the assistant should ask first.

## 4. The plate override

I meant it as a fact, and it has one small consequence. If someone has set, say, print order on a specific plate through Plate Settings, then changing the process value does nothing for that plate, yet the tool reports "applied". That only arises when a per-plate value exists, which is uncommon. A warning in the result naming the overriding plate would close it. I read the merge order in the code but did not test it.

## 5. A small blacklist

Agreed. The criteria I would propose for it:

- **Runs a program on the computer:** `post_process`.
- **Holds a secret or a network target:** the print host address, API key, user and password. The other session is checking whether those are readable today.
- **Sends raw commands to the machine:** custom G-code. This is currently allowed for printer and filament, so it is your call whether it belongs on the blacklist or stays allowed with the person's approval.
change whitelist to blacklist with the small blacklist you recommended. spin up a task chip for discussing how we can deal with the edit time questions

input.tldr: The settings tools can now change almost any setting, including about ten where OrcaSlicer asks a person a question when they edit the field. A tool change skips that question. This session would lay out the options for each one and bring a recommendation to discuss, without building anything yet.
input.prompt:
This is a design discussion with Kenneth, not an implementation task. Produce a short proposal with options and a recommendation, then stop and discuss. Do not change code until Kenneth picks a direction. Do not run tests that call a live model.

Repository /Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin, branch jusprin-newui. Read agent-docs/jusprin/README.md, agent-docs/jusprin/product-definition.md (who owns which decisions: the user owns physical facts, object meaning and desired outcomes; the agent chooses the technical strategy) and agent-docs/jusprin/mcp-tool-extension-guide.md, section "Settings tools: contract and hazards".

Background. On 2026-10-12 the settings tools' write policy changed from per-scope allow-lists to one blacklist (blocked_setting in src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Workspace/SettingsSupport.hpp). That change is UNCOMMITTED in another session's worktree at /Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/.claude/worktrees/spiral-vase-writable (branch claude/spiral-vase-writable). You may read files there; do not edit or build there. Check first whether it has since been committed or merged into jusprin-newui. In that worktree the guide's hazard section ends with a paragraph "Not covered by any guard" that names this open question.

The problem. Tool changes go through Tab::load_config, which does not run Tab::on_value_change (src/slic3r/GUI/Tab.cpp, roughly lines 1495 to 1960). on_value_change is where OrcaSlicer asks a person a question when they edit certain fields. So a tool change to these settings applies silently where the app would have asked. Verified on the real app over MCP: a patch setting timelapse_type=1 and make_overhang_printable=1 applied with no question and no warning.

The questions, as read from the code on 2026-10-12, with a first classification:
- support_interface_filament: "apply the recommended companion settings?" (0 top Z distance, 0 interface spacing, interlaced rectilinear, independent support layer height off, sometimes support_filament too). Technical; the agent could send them together.
- enable_prime_tower turned off while timelapse_type is smooth, or while enable_wrapping_detection is on: "are you sure". Technical dependency.
- enable_prime_tower on with precise_z_height, and precise_z_height on with the prime tower: "may cause slicing errors". Technical.
- enable_wrapping_detection on without a prime tower. Technical.
- timelapse_type smooth without a prime tower: "enable the prime tower?". Technical once a timelapse is wanted.
- sparse_infill_rotate_template on a pattern not designed for rotation. Technical.
- layer_height outside the nozzle's limits: "adjust automatically?". Already refused by the existing guard for the maximum; check the minimum.
- support_filament set to a non-soluble support material: "not recommended for support base". Mostly technical, but depends on which spools are really loaded.
- print_sequence by object on a bed-slinger (printer_structure i3): timelapse in traditional mode is lost. Mildly a user preference.
- make_overhang_printable: "will modify the model's shape"; matters when dimensions or fit matter. The user's decision.
- long_retractions_when_cut and filament_long_retractions_when_cut: experimental, may raise the risk of clogs. Accepting a risk to the printer; the user's decision.
Re-read on_value_change to confirm this list is complete for the process, filament and printer tabs, and note each condition exactly.

Existing pattern to build on. Spiral vase is handled by the preview: check_process_dialogs in src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Workspace/OrcaSettings.hpp refuses spiral_mode alone and names the companion values to send in the same patch. Preview results already have "issues" (blocking) and "warnings" (non-blocking, e.g. normalized_dependency). The fork also has ScopedDialogListener (src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Workspace/DialogListeners.hpp), which can intercept and answer OrcaSlicer dialogs.

Options to weigh, per question rather than one rule for all:
1. Preview warning that states the condition and names the companion settings; the agent decides.
2. Blocking issue until the companion settings are in the same patch (the spiral vase treatment).
3. Blocking issue that tells the agent to ask the person first, for the questions that belong to the user; decide how the tool learns the person agreed.
4. Put the setting on the blacklist.
5. Call OrcaSlicer's own handler with a dialog listener answering, so OrcaSlicer applies its own companion changes.
Consider how each keeps the tool honest (the result must say what really changed), how it survives an upstream rebase (the conditions live in Tab.cpp, which upstream edits), and how each would be tested against the real workspace adapter (tests/workspace/real_adapter_harness.cpp has a sweep, verify_every_writable_setting, and tests/shell/shell_harness.cpp has per-feature checks).

---
name: settings-write-blacklist
description: "2026-10-12 decision: settings tools write everything except one blacklist (blocked_setting); what goes on it, the sweep that proves the rest, and that it sat uncommitted on claude/spiral-vase-writable"
metadata:
  type: project
---

On 2026-10-12 Kenneth replaced the settings tools' three per-scope write allow-lists with one blacklist: `blocked_setting` in `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Workspace/SettingsSupport.hpp`. Everything else a scope holds is writable.

**What goes on the blacklist (Kenneth agreed to "a small blacklist for genuinely dangerous ops"):** runs a program (`post_process`); printer network address and sign-in (`print_host`, `printhost_*`); preset identity and compatibility (`inherits`, `compatible_*`, `*_extruder_variant`, `printer_technology`); printer hardware (model, bed, nozzles, extruders), which stays with `printer_setup` / `printer_change`. 51 keys: 6 process, 6 filament, 43 printer. The last two groups were my addition beyond the three criteria I had proposed to him; they preserve the earlier recorded decision that settings calls never change topology. Custom g-code stayed writable (I offered it as his call; he did not answer, so existing behaviour was kept).

**Why:** the allow-list's five original reasons (dialog, silent rewrite, slicing/dirty state, Undo, concurrent edits) are all guarded for any key now. The dialog guards check the whole configuration, not the patch's keys.

**How to apply:** do not add a key to the blacklist because Orca asks about it or rewrites it; that is the guards' job. The proof is the sweep `verify_every_writable_setting` in `tests/workspace/real_adapter_harness.cpp` (every setting of three scopes through preview, apply, inverse; 340 process, 92 filament, 112 printer applied and restored, no dialog). Run it after an upstream update. Known harmless oddities it shows: `machine_max_junction_deviation` defaults to `0.01f` and comes back as a different double (preset stays marked changed); `silent_mode` is a retired key Orca drops.

**Open:** about ten settings whose question Orca asks only in `Tab::on_value_change` (prime tower with timelapse, by-object sequence, `make_overhang_printable`, support filaments) now apply with no question. Kenneth asked for a separate discussion task on that. # Finding: settings_get returned print host credentials (2026-10-12)

Branch `claude/upbeat-pike-4b6d66`, based on `jusprin-newui` d0bce03db3. Changes are uncommitted.

## Problem

The MCP and in-app tool `settings_get` returned a printer preset's stored connection secrets. I put dummy values in a throwaway user printer preset and called the tool through the shell harness (`--manual-mcp`): it returned all seven, including `printhost_apikey` and `printhost_password`.

- `settings_search` never returns values, only definitions. `settings_preview_patch` refuses these keys without showing a value. `workspace_inspect` shows nothing.
- A user printer keeps host address, API key, user and password in its preset file. JusPrin's own connect flow asks for the key in a local form so the model never sees it, then saves it to `printhost_apikey`, which `settings_get` read back (code reading).
- A Bambu access code is kept in the app config file, per device, not in a preset. No tool returns it (code reading, not run live).

## Solution (implemented)

`settings_get` now refuses seven printer keys: `print_host`, `print_host_webui`, `printhost_apikey`, `printhost_cafile`, `printhost_user`, `printhost_password`, `printhost_port`. Each comes back under `unknownKeys` with code `withheld_setting`; other keys in the same call are still read. Search still lists them.

This is the list OrcaSlicer already strips from G-code, project files and exported presets. The list lives once in `SettingsSupport.hpp` and is applied in `read_settings` of the real and the fake workspace adapter, below both tool adapters. No schema or catalog change. No file outside `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/`, tests and the guide changed.

## Tests and results

- Reproduction script before the fix: 7 dummy values returned. After: 7 `withheld_setting` issues, no dummy value in any reply.
- Unit tests: workspace contract 316 assertions, agent tests 4831 assertions, all pass. The two new tests fail when the guard is removed.
- Real adapter harness: 975 checks, 0 failed (4 new).
- Shell harness over real TCP (`--mcp`): 100 checks, 0 failed (1 new). Default shell regression: 529 checks, 0 failed.
- Not run: Python bridge tests, AgentUI tests, Windows, any live model.

## Remaining issues

1. Your decision: the address keys are withheld too, because a host URL can hold `user:password@` and OrcaSlicer treats them as sensitive. Narrowing to API key, user and password is a one-line change.
2. The printer chat's connection status tool sends the saved host address to the model as stored. An address saved in OrcaSlicer's dialog with `user:password@` in it would leak there. Not reproduced, not fixed.
3. An unsaved edit to a host key appears with both values in the setup card and the change log, which is saved with the project's conversation. I found no path from there to the model. Code reading only.
4. Other readable free text, left readable because the tools exist to read and edit it: process `post_process` (script paths and arguments, which can hold tokens and show the home folder name), `notes`, `filename_format`; filament notes and g-code; printer notes, twelve custom g-code keys, `bed_custom_texture` and `bed_custom_model` (file paths), `flashforge_serial_number`. `post_process` is the one I would consider withholding next.

table of types, enum values, ranges, units, or aliases.
6. Search and read cover every setting definition that applies to the
   requested scope, and every one of them is writable except the keys on
   one blacklist (`blocked_setting` in `SettingsSupport.hpp`). Every record
   returned by search or read says whether the key is writable. Trying to
   change a blocked key returns `unsupported_setting_mutation`. A key goes
   on the blacklist for what a wrong value does outside the print:
   - it runs a program on the computer (`post_process`);
   - it says where a printer is on the network, or how to sign in to it;
   - it records which preset this is, what it inherits from and what it
     fits, so that a different value breaks the preset;
   - it is the printer's hardware (model, bed, nozzles, extruders), which
     decides which filaments and processes fit and how many values a
     per-extruder setting holds. Those change with `printer_setup` or
     `printer_change`.

   A setting does not go on the blacklist because OrcaSlicer asks about it
   or rewrites it. Those are handled for every key by the guards and the
   sweep described under
   [the process normalizer](#the-process-normalizer-can-open-dialogs-and-rewrite-values).

   History: until 2026-10-12 each scope had a reviewed allowlist (40 of 356
   process settings, 34 filament, 35 printer), and a key was added only
   after an audit of its own. The audit guarded against five things: a
   dialog, a silent rewrite, slicing and dirty state, Undo, and edits made
   at the same time. All five are now guarded for any key, so Kenneth
   replaced the allowlists with the blacklist.

   One exception to "read covers every definition": the seven printer keys
   that say where a print host is and how to sign in to it (`print_host`,
   `print_host_webui`, `printhost_apikey`, `printhost_cafile`,
   `printhost_user`, `printhost_password`, `printhost_port`). Search lists

Yes, it was a small fix, and it is done. The commit is rebased onto the remote's newer commit, amended to include the credential-read fix, and pushed as `5dadfe2801`. Local and remote `jusprin-newui` are in sync.

## What the amended commit now contains

- **The blacklist change**, as before.
- **The read fix, ported from the other session.** Two source files, about 27 lines, plus its tests. `settings_get` no longer returns seven printer connection settings: host address, web address, API key, user, password, CA file and port. Each comes back marked as withheld, and the other settings in the same call are still read.
- **The commit message** now has a section on why blocking writes did not stop the leak, and what was done.

**On the 7-or-13 question:** I kept the read block at 7, as the other session recommended. The other six in that group hold no address or credential, so they stay readable. Say so if you would rather use all 13.

Porting meant resolving the two conflicts that session reported (the tool guide and the test fake) and updating its one test for the changed function. I also taught my every-setting test to expect those seven as unreadable.

## Test results on the combined result

| Test | Result |
|---|---|
| Workspace contract tests | 317 assertions, all pass |
| Agent tests | 5073 assertions, all pass |
| Workspace harness, including the every-setting test and the new "seeded host key is withheld" checks | 3166 checks, 0 failures |
| Shell harness over the app's real tool endpoint | 100 checks, 0 failures |
| Shell harness full regression | 547 checks, 0 failures on the final build (2 clean runs of 3) |

**Two shell harness runs were not clean, and I did not find out why.** Both were in places this change does not touch, and reruns passed:

- One run, on the rebased build before the read fix, stalled waiting for the test assistant's reply in a second conversation. The rerun passed.
- One run on the final build failed a single keyboard-focus check on the header chip. The next two runs passed.

My guess is that the focus one is from the Mac being in use while the test window was open, and the stall may relate to the remote's new commit, since four runs before the rebase had none. I have not tested either guess. Both are recorded in the commit message.

Not run: Windows, the Python bridge tests, the page tests, and any live model.

## Two things to do on your side

- **The other session still holds its own uncommitted copy of the read fix** in the worktree `upbeat-pike-4b6d66`. Its changes are now in `5dadfe2801`, so it should discard its copy and not merge it. Its finding file `settings-credentials-finding.md` is still there, untracked.
- **That session's remaining issues are still open.** The main one: the printer chat's connection status tool sends the saved host address to the model, so an address saved with a user and password inside it would still leak there. It was not reproduced and is not fixed.
